quickAnswer: Most Indian traditions accept rebirth (samsara) shaped by karma, and see liberation as release from that cycle; they differ on what continues. Vedantic schools say the Self does not die and the subtle body carries karmic impressions to a new birth; Jainism speaks of a soul bound by karmic matter; Buddhism describes rebirth as a causal continuity without a permanent self. The Charvaka materialists denied any afterlife, and Sikh thought places the cycle under divine will and grace.

perspectives.view: The Katha Upanishad is framed as a young man's questions to Death, who teaches that the Self is not killed when the body is killed.
Vedanta holds that at death the subtle body (sukshma sharira), carrying desires and impressions, leaves the gross body and takes on another, until knowledge or grace ends the cycle.
Jainism teaches that the soul, weighed by its karmic matter, moves immediately into a new birth among the many realms of beings; the freed soul rises to the summit of the universe.
Buddhism teaches rebirth without a transmigrating self: craving and intention condition a new arising, like a flame lit from another flame.
The Charvaka or Lokayata materialists held that consciousness arises from the body and ends with it; they rejected rebirth and the afterlife.
Sikh thought accepts the cycle of birth and death but emphasises that human life is a rare chance to merge with God through the Name and grace.

goDeeper.note: What is born must die and what dies is reborn — so do not grieve over the inevitable.
What one dwells on at the time of death shapes what follows.
The self carries the senses and mind like the wind carries scent.
The cycle of rebirth across the traditions.
